nodes.label: Sasanian Mesopotamia
nodes.full: What the conquest inherits: Ctesiphon and the Sawad, the kharāg tax system, the dihqān landlords, the rabbinic academies and the catholicos, the canal network at its height. See mesopotamia-224-637.
nodes.src: background — see the folio mesopotamia-224-637.

nodes.label: Buyid and Seljuk Iraq
nodes.full: The warlord centuries that follow 945 — the caliph a pensioner, the Sawad's canals decaying, Iraq the contested prize of Buyid, then Seljuk, then Mongol armies. See iraq-945-1258.
nodes.src: background — see the folio iraq-945-1258.

nodes.label: The Caliphate as empire
nodes.full: The imperial state whose capital Iraq holds — the caliph, the guard, the revenue of three continents, the provinces from al-Andalus to Sind, the theory of the deputy of God. See caliphate-750-945.
nodes.src: background — see the folio caliphate-750-945.

nodes.label: Khurasan and the East
nodes.full: Where the Abbasid revolution, the Turkish soldiery, the paper technology and much of the secretarial class came from — the eastern half that Baghdad governed and drew its strength from.
nodes.src: background — Hugh Kennedy, 'The Early Abbasid Caliphate' (1981).

nodes.label: The wider world
nodes.full: al-Andalus, the Maghrib, Byzantium, the India and China sea routes, the Volga and the Baltic — the routes and correspondents that made Baghdad the acknowledged centre of the inhabited world.
nodes.src: background — Ibn Khurradadhbih, 'Kitāb al-Masālik wa-l-Mamālik'.

nodes.label: The conquest and the founding of Kufa and Basra
nodes.full: Within two years of al-Qadisiyya the Arab armies laid out two garrison cities on the desert edge — Basra near the head of the Gulf, Kufa near the ruins of al-Hira — as bases from which to hold the Sawad and push into Iran. They filled with tribesmen drawing a state stipend, and within a generation they were the two largest and most turbulent cities of the Muslim world.
nodes.src: al-Baladhuri, 'Futūḥ al-Buldān'; al-Tabari I; Hichem Djaït, 'Al-Kūfa: naissance de la ville islamique' (1986).

nodes.label: Kufa the capital of Ali and the home of dissent
nodes.full: Ali moved the caliphate to Kufa in 656 and was murdered in its mosque five years later. The city stayed the centre of loyalty to his house and of every grievance against Damascus: it invited al-Husayn to his death at Karbala, rose for the Penitents and then for al-Mukhtar, and gave the Umayyads' governors their hardest problem for the next sixty years.
nodes.src: al-Tabari II; Wilferd Madelung, 'The Succession to Muhammad' (1997).

nodes.label: al-Hajjaj and the Umayyad grip
nodes.full: The Umayyads ruled Iraq through hard men — Ziyad ibn Abihi, then al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf, who governed for twenty years by terror. He broke the great revolt of the Iraqi army under Ibn al-Ash'ath, built a fresh garrison city, Wasit, midway between Kufa and Basra to hold Syrian troops apart from the Iraqis, and reformed the coinage and the canals. Iraq paid, and hated him.
nodes.src: al-Tabari II; al-Baladhuri, 'Ansāb al-Ashrāf'; the foundation of Wasit in Yāqūt.

nodes.label: The Abbasids come to power from Kufa
nodes.full: The revolution that overthrew the Umayyads was made in Khurasan but proclaimed in Iraq: in October 749 the Abbasid Abu al-Abbas was hailed as caliph in the mosque of Kufa. His brother al-Mansur, who really built the dynasty, distrusted the Kufans as much as any Umayyad had, and looked for a capital of his own.
nodes.src: al-Tabari III; Hugh Kennedy, 'The Early Abbasid Caliphate' (1981).

nodes.label: al-Mansur builds Baghdad
nodes.full: In 762 al-Mansur laid out a perfectly round walled city on the west bank of the Tigris, a few miles up from the ruins of Ctesiphon, and named it the City of Peace. The palace and the great mosque stood at the centre, the four gates faced the four roads of the empire, and within fifty years the built-up area had spilled far beyond the walls into the largest city west of China.
nodes.src: al-Ya'qubi, 'Kitāb al-Buldān'; al-Khatib al-Baghdadi, 'Ta'rīkh Baghdād'; Jacob Lassner, 'The Topography of Baghdad in the Early Middle Ages' (1970).

nodes.label: The golden age and the war for Baghdad
nodes.full: Under Harun al-Rashid and al-Ma'mun the city was the hub of the world's wealth and learning — and then, in 812–813, the arena of a year-long siege, as al-Ma'mun's armies from the east stormed the capital of his brother al-Amin, who was caught and killed. Al-Ma'mun stayed away for six years and came back to a city that had begun its long habit of destroying itself.
nodes.src: al-Tabari III; the siege poems of al-Khuraymi; Michael Cooperson, 'Al-Maʾmun' (2005).

nodes.label: al-Mu'tasim, the Turks and Samarra
nodes.full: To house a new army of Turkish and Central Asian slave-soldiers apart from a resentful Baghdad, al-Mu'tasim built a second capital sixty miles up the Tigris at Samarra in 836. It became a byword for the state's captivity to its own guard: between 861 and 870 the soldiers murdered four caliphs in a decade. The court returned to Baghdad in 892, leaving Samarra to shrink back to a village.
nodes.src: al-Ya'qubi, 'Kitāb al-Buldān'; Matthew Gordon, 'The Breaking of a Thousand Swords' (2001); Alastair Northedge, 'The Historical Topography of Samarra' (2005).

nodes.label: Power passes to the wazirs and the amir al-umara
nodes.full: After a brief recovery under al-Mu'tadid the caliphate ran out of money and out of soldiers it could trust. Rival bureaucratic clans fought over the vizierate; then in 936 the office of amir al-umara, commander of commanders, handed real power to whichever general held Baghdad. In December 945 that general was a Buyid from the Caspian, and the caliph became his pensioner.
nodes.src: Miskawayh, 'Tajārib al-Umam'; Harold Bowen, 'The Life and Times of ʿAlī ibn ʿĪsā' (1928).

nodes.label: The Camel, Siffin and Nahrawan
nodes.full: The first war among Muslims was fought largely on Iraqi ground. Ali beat a rival army outside Basra at the Battle of the Camel in 656, faced Mu'awiya's Syrians to a standstill at Siffin on the upper Euphrates in 657, and then turned on his own hardliners — the first Kharijites — and destroyed them at Nahrawan near the future Baghdad in 658. Iraq was left permanently split.
nodes.src: al-Tabari I; al-Minqari, 'Waqʿat Ṣiffīn'; Wilferd Madelung (1997).

nodes.label: Karbala and the Kufan revolts
nodes.full: Invited by the Kufans and then abandoned by them, the Prophet's grandson al-Husayn was surrounded and killed with his small party on the plain of Karbala on the tenth of Muharram, 680. The guilt of it drove two Kufan risings within a decade — the Penitents, and then al-Mukhtar's movement in the name of another son of Ali — and made martyrdom and the pilgrimage to the grave the core of Shia devotion.
nodes.src: al-Tabari II; Abu Mikhnaf's 'Maqtal al-Ḥusayn'; Mahmoud Ayoub, 'Redemptive Suffering in Islam' (1978).

nodes.label: Ibn al-Ash'ath and the army's revolt
nodes.full: Sent east to fight in Sistan, the Iraqi army turned around, marched home, and rose against al-Hajjaj and the Umayyad state — joined by many of the Quran-reciters and jurists of Kufa and Basra. Al-Hajjaj broke them at Dayr al-Jamajim in 701 with Syrian troops and then hunted the leaders down. It was the last time the old Iraqi military class tried to set the terms of its own service.
nodes.src: al-Tabari II; Redwan Sayed, 'Die Revolte des Ibn al-Ashʿath' (1977).

nodes.label: The siege of Baghdad
nodes.full: When the brothers al-Amin and al-Ma'mun fell out, al-Ma'mun's Khurasani general Tahir besieged the capital for more than a year. Catapults battered the round city, the suburbs burned, and irregular bands of the poor — the 'naked ones' — did much of the fighting for al-Amin. He was taken trying to flee across the river and killed. It was the first sack of Baghdad, by its own empire.
nodes.src: al-Tabari III; the eyewitness verses of al-Khuraymi in al-Ṭabari; John Nawas on the civil war.

nodes.label: The Zanj rebellion in the marshes
nodes.full: East African slaves cutting the nitrous crust off the salt flats of lower Iraq for wages that never came rose in 869 under a man who claimed descent from Ali. For fourteen years they held the marshes, built a capital, minted coins, sacked Basra in 871 with great slaughter, and threatened Baghdad. The regent al-Muwaffaq finally ground them down in 883. It was the largest slave revolt before modern times.
nodes.src: al-Tabari III; Alexandre Popović, 'The Revolt of African Slaves in Iraq' (1999).

nodes.label: The Qaramita and the helpless caliphate
nodes.full: An Ismaili preacher organised the peasants of the Sawad around Kufa in the 870s; the movement built a raiding state on the Gulf coast that in the 900s cut the pilgrim roads, defeated caliphal armies, and in 930 stormed Mecca during the hajj, massacred the pilgrims, and carried off the Black Stone. That the caliphate could do nothing about it for twenty years measured how far it had fallen.
nodes.src: al-Tabari III; Miskawayh; Wilferd Madelung, 'Fatimiden und Bahrainqarmaten' (1959).

nodes.label: The amsar and the stipend register
nodes.full: Kufa and Basra began as tribal cantonments — quarters assigned by clan, a governor's residence and a mosque at the centre, and a register, the diwan, that paid every fighting man an annual stipend graded by precedence in Islam. The stipend, not land, was the reward of conquest. As the money and the tribesmen settled, the camps hardened into cities of a quarter-million and more.
nodes.src: al-Baladhuri, 'Futūḥ al-Buldān'; Fred Donner, 'The Early Islamic Conquests' (1981); Hichem Djaït (1986).

nodes.label: The Sawad kept as a common endowment
nodes.full: The caliph Umar refused to divide the conquered farmland of the Sawad among the soldiers; it was left with its cultivators as fayʾ, a permanent endowment for the whole community, taxed by the Sasanian survey the conquerors had inherited. The old crown estates became the caliph's sawafi. Al-Hajjaj later tried to pin the peasants to the land and tax converts like everyone else — a policy that helped make Iraq ungovernable.
nodes.src: Abu Yusuf, 'Kitāb al-Kharāj'; Michael Morony, 'Iraq after the Muslim Conquest' (1984).

nodes.label: Baghdad as the machine of empire
nodes.full: The imperial capital ran on a dense apparatus: the caliphal palace-cities on both banks, the chief judge over a network of qadis, the market inspector policing weights and morals, the police, the postmaster who was also the caliph's spy, and a treasury drawing on the revenue of three continents. Feeding and ordering a city of half a million was itself a feat of government.
nodes.src: al-Khatib al-Baghdadi, 'Ta'rīkh Baghdād'; Jacob Lassner, 'The Shaping of ʿAbbāsid Rule' (1980).

nodes.label: The wazirate and the diwans
nodes.full: The Abbasids ran their empire through a vizier and a set of ministries — land tax, army, chancery, seal, posts — staffed by a professional secretarial class, the kuttab, largely of Persian and Christian background and trained in an Iranian tradition of statecraft. The Barmakid family, viziers for a generation under Harun al-Rashid, showed both the reach of the office and how fast a caliph could destroy its holders.
nodes.src: al-Jahshiyari, 'Kitāb al-Wuzarāʾ wa-l-Kuttāb'; Dominique Sourdel, 'Le vizirat ʿabbāside' (1959).

nodes.label: The qadi and the making of fiqh
nodes.full: Early on a judge decided by the governor's instructions and his own sense of right. Over two generations the jurists of Kufa and Basra turned that into a system — a body of reasoned law with its own methods and its own teachers. Abu Hanifa and his students in Kufa, working by analogy and considered opinion, produced the first great school; the writing-down of law had begun.
nodes.src: al-Shaybani, 'Kitāb al-Aṣl'; Joseph Schacht, 'The Origins of Muhammadan Jurisprudence' (1950); Wael Hallaq, 'The Origins and Evolution of Islamic Law' (2005).

nodes.label: The dhimma and its communal heads
nodes.full: Jews, Christians, Mandaeans and Zoroastrians lived as protected non-Muslims — paying the poll tax, barred from certain offices and dress, but self-governing under leaders the caliph recognised by diploma: the exilarch for the Jews, the catholicos for the Church of the East. The arrangement continued the Sasanian pattern. It could tighten sharply, as under al-Mutawakkil's edicts of 850.
nodes.src: al-Tabari III (al-Mutawakkil's edicts); Milka Levy-Rubin, 'Non-Muslims in the Early Islamic Empire' (2011).

nodes.label: Kufa, Basra and the birth of the madhhab
nodes.full: The two garrison cities became the two poles of early Islamic legal thought. Kufa was the home of raʾy — disciplined reasoned opinion, worked out from principle where the texts ran short — and of Abu Hanifa, whose circle produced the first school to outlast its founder. The habit of arguing law in named, competing traditions, the madhhab system, starts here.
nodes.src: Nurit Tsafrir, 'The History of an Islamic School of Law: The Early Spread of Hanafism' (2004); Christopher Melchert, 'The Formation of the Sunni Schools of Law' (1997).

nodes.label: The traditionists and the isnad
nodes.full: Against the reasoners rose the people of hadith, who held that the only sound guide beyond the Quran was an authenticated report of what the Prophet said or did, each carried by a named chain of transmitters back to an eyewitness. Basra was a great centre of the collecting and the sifting, and of the vast biographical science that grew up to judge which transmitters could be trusted.
nodes.src: Jonathan Brown, 'Hadith: Muhammad's Legacy in the Medieval and Modern World' (2009).

nodes.label: The shrines and the Occultation
nodes.full: Shia Islam grew up in the soil of Kufa. Over these centuries its holy geography took form on Iraqi ground: the grave of Ali at Najaf, identified in the late 700s; Karbala, where al-Husayn fell; the tombs of two imams at al-Kazimayn in Baghdad; and Samarra, where the eleventh imam died and the twelfth was said to have gone into hiding in 874, and then into a total concealment in 941 that still holds.
nodes.src: Heinz Halm, 'Shiʿism' (1991); Moojan Momen, 'An Introduction to Shiʿi Islam' (1985).

nodes.label: The Mutazila and the Inquisition
nodes.full: A school of theologians that began in Basra held that reason could establish God's justice and unity — and that the Quran, being an act of God rather than a part of him, was created in time. In 833 al-Ma'mun made assent to the created Quran a test of office and imprisoned those who refused, Ahmad ibn Hanbal chief among them. The Inquisition failed; when it was lifted in 848 the traditionists had won the argument in the street.
nodes.src: al-Tabari III; Josef van Ess, 'Theologie und Gesellschaft' (1991–97); John Nawas on the mihna.

nodes.label: The geonim and the catholicos at their height
nodes.full: With the court at Baghdad the two great institutions of the protected faiths reached their peak there. The Jewish academies of Sura and Pumbedita, now in the capital, sent legal rulings to communities from Spain to India, and Saadia Gaon translated the Bible into Arabic and beat back the Karaite challenge. The Nestorian patriarch Timothy I debated theology with al-Mahdi and dispatched bishops toward China.
nodes.src: Robert Brody, 'The Geonim of Babylonia' (1998); the 'Apology of Timothy'; Sebastian Brock (2000).

nodes.label: From the Basran ascetics to al-Hallaj
nodes.full: Muslim mysticism took shape in Iraq. It began with the fear-filled asceticism of al-Hasan al-Basri's Basra and Rabiʿa's teaching of pure love of God, and matured in Baghdad into a disciplined path — al-Junayd's careful, 'sober' Sufism. Its limit was tested by al-Hallaj, who spoke of union with God in the first person and was crucified in Baghdad in 922.
nodes.src: Louis Massignon, 'The Passion of al-Hallāj' (tr. 1982); Ahmet Karamustafa, 'Sufism: The Formative Period' (2007).

nodes.label: The grammarians of Basra and Kufa
nodes.full: As Arabic became the language of a non-Arab empire, scholars in the two garrison cities set out to fix its rules. Al-Khalil ibn Ahmad of Basra compiled the first dictionary and codified the metres of poetry; his Persian pupil Sibawayh wrote a grammar so complete it was simply called The Book. The Kufan school challenged the Basrans point by point, and out of the quarrel came classical Arabic.
nodes.src: Sibawayh, 'al-Kitāb'; Michael Carter, 'Sibawayhi' (2004); the Basra–Kufa debate in al-Anbari's 'al-Inṣāf'.

nodes.label: Adab and the prose of the salon
nodes.full: A new kind of writing — witty, digressive, encyclopedic, meant to make a cultivated man good company — took shape in Abbasid Iraq. Ibn al-Muqaffa turned the Persian mirror-for-princes and the Indian fable book into Arabic prose; al-Jahiz of Basra wrote on everything from misers to the anatomy of animals with the same restless irony. This adab set the standard of educated Arabic for a thousand years.
nodes.src: al-Jahiz, 'Kitāb al-Ḥayawān' and 'al-Bukhalāʾ'; Ibn al-Muqaffaʿ, 'Kalīla wa-Dimna'.

nodes.label: The poets of the Baghdad court
nodes.full: The court and its patrons drew the best poets of the age to Baghdad, and they broke with the desert conventions: Abu Nuwas made wine, the city and self-mockery into high art; Abu Tammam and al-Buhturi built the ornate badiʿ style of dense metaphor. Poetry was a career — a good ode could be worth a fortune — and the caliph's praise or displeasure made and ruined reputations.
nodes.src: the 'Dīwān' of Abu Nuwas; Suzanne Stetkevych, 'Abū Tammām and the Poetics of the ʿAbbāsid Age' (1991).

nodes.label: Paper, the warraqin and the book trade
nodes.full: Paper reached Baghdad from Samarkand and the first mill opened around 795; within a century the trade in books had a street of its own, the Market of the Stationers near the Basra Gate, where copyists sold, authors dictated, and scholars met. The bookseller Ibn al-Nadim's catalogue of everything then available in Arabic lists thousands of titles. No pre-modern society produced books on this scale.
nodes.src: Ibn al-Nadim, 'al-Fihrist'; Jonathan Bloom, 'Paper Before Print' (2001).

nodes.label: The Round City and the Samarra style
nodes.full: Al-Mansur's Baghdad was a perfect circle, a plan with no real precedent or sequel, its palace and mosque ringed by two miles of double wall. Samarra was the opposite — a strip city thirty kilometres long, its Great Mosque fronted by the spiral Malwiya minaret, its palaces sheathed in moulded stucco cut in a slanted, endlessly repeatable pattern. That Samarra style travelled from Egypt to Central Asia.
nodes.src: Alastair Northedge, 'The Historical Topography of Samarra' (2005); Jacob Lassner, 'The Topography of Baghdad' (1970).

nodes.label: Greek learning into Arabic
nodes.full: Over four generations nearly the whole of Greek science and philosophy that survived was turned into Arabic, mostly through Syriac, by teams of salaried translators — the Christian physician Hunayn ibn Ishaq's workshop the most exacting of them. Caliphs, viziers and rich families paid for it, sometimes by the weight of the finished book. It was a sustained public project, not a scattering of curiosity.
nodes.src: Dimitri Gutas, 'Greek Thought, Arabic Culture' (1998); the 'Risāla' of Hunayn ibn Ishaq on his Galen translations.

nodes.label: al-Kindi and the first Arabic philosophy
nodes.full: Al-Kindi, an Arab nobleman at the courts of al-Ma'mun and al-Mu'tasim, was the first to do philosophy in Arabic — arguing that the truths of Greek metaphysics and of revelation were one, and writing on optics, music, medicine, cryptanalysis and the making of perfumes besides. He set the pattern of the Muslim philosopher as a universal scientist working under a patron.
nodes.src: al-Kindi, 'On First Philosophy'; Peter Adamson, 'Al-Kindī' (2007).

nodes.label: al-Khwarizmi and the sciences of number
nodes.full: Working in al-Ma'mun's circle, al-Khwarizmi wrote the book that named and founded algebra, a treatise that carried the Indian decimal numerals into the Arabic world — and, through a Latin garble of his name, gave Europe the word algorithm — and a set of astronomical tables blending Indian and Greek method. Alongside him the Banu Musa brothers worked on geometry and machines.
nodes.src: al-Khwarizmi, 'al-Kitāb al-mukhtaṣar fī ḥisāb al-jabr wa-l-muqābala'; Roshdi Rashed, 'Al-Khwārizmī: The Beginnings of Algebra' (2009).

nodes.label: Medicine and the Baghdad hospital
nodes.full: The physicians of Gondeshapur came to court with the Abbasids, and around 805 a hospital on the Persian model was built in Baghdad under Barmakid patronage — a teaching institution with wards, a pharmacy and a staff. Hunayn's translations gave Arabic the whole Galenic corpus; a century later al-Razi, directing a Baghdad hospital, added a lifetime of case notes and clinical judgement.
nodes.src: Ibn Abi Usaybia, 'ʿUyūn al-Anbāʾ'; al-Razi, 'al-Ḥāwī'; Peter Pormann & Emilie Savage-Smith, 'Medieval Islamic Medicine' (2007).

nodes.label: History and geography become disciplines
nodes.full: Baghdad's scholars invented the large-scale forms of both fields. Al-Tabari compiled a history of the world from the creation to his own day, year by year, quoting his sources; al-Baladhuri wrote the story of the conquests; and the postmaster Ibn Khurradadhbih turned his official knowledge of the roads and revenues into the first Arabic geography of routes. History and geography were now organised sciences with methods.
nodes.src: al-Tabari, 'Ta'rīkh al-Rusul wa-l-Mulūk'; Ibn Khurradadhbih, 'Kitāb al-Masālik wa-l-Mamālik'; Chase Robinson, 'Islamic Historiography' (2003).

nodes.label: The Sawad's peak and the new crops
nodes.full: For a century and a half after the conquest the canal country was kept up and pushed further, and a wave of crops moved in from India and Iran through Iraq to the rest of the Muslim world — rice, sugar cane, cotton, citrus, aubergine, hard wheat, watermelon — many of them grown through the hot months on irrigation. Iraq was the empire's granary and the doorway through which its farming was transformed.
nodes.src: Andrew Watson, 'Agricultural Innovation in the Early Islamic World' (1983); Michael Morony on the Sawad economy.

nodes.label: Baghdad and the instruments of finance
nodes.full: A city of half a million on a gold-and-silver currency generated a sophisticated money trade: money-changers who took deposits and made payments, a bill of exchange, the suftaja, that let a merchant carry credit from Baghdad to Morocco without carrying coin, and the written payment order — the sakk — from which the word cheque descends. The financial plumbing of the medieval world was laid here.
nodes.src: Abraham Udovitch, 'Partnership and Profit in Medieval Islam' (1970); the jahbadh in Miskawayh and W. Fischel.

nodes.label: Basra, Siraf and the sea road to China
nodes.full: From Basra and its outport, and from Siraf on the Persian shore, Iraqi and Persian ships ran the monsoon route to Malabar, Sri Lanka and Canton and came back with teak, pepper, aromatics, silk and porcelain. An account written at Basra in 851 describes the Chinese ports and customs in detail. It is the world of the Sindbad tales, and it made Basra the richest commercial city of the age.
nodes.src: 'Akhbār al-Ṣīn wa-l-Hind' (851, tr. as 'Accounts of China and India'); George Hourani, 'Arab Seafaring' (1951).

nodes.label: The failing treasury and the coming of the iqta
nodes.full: As revenue fell and soldiers went unpaid, the state stopped paying cash and started handing over the tax of a district directly to an officer to collect for himself — the iqtaʿ. Tax-farmers and the caliph's relatives took the rest. Within two generations the fisc was carved into military assignments, the treasury was a shell, and whoever controlled the soldiers controlled Iraq.
nodes.src: Claude Cahen, 'L'évolution de l'iqṭāʿ' (1953); Hugh Kennedy, 'The Decline and Fall of the First Muslim Empire' (in Der Islam 1998).

nodes.label: The salt marsh and the Zanj labour system
nodes.full: Absentee investors in Basra bought tracts of the salt-crusted lowland south of the city and set gangs of enslaved East Africans to strip off the nitrous surface layer, dig drainage, and plant. The men were worked in the heat on a ration of flour and dates. It was the nearest thing the medieval Middle East had to plantation slavery, and in 869 it blew up into the Zanj war.
nodes.src: al-Tabari III; Alexandre Popović, 'The Revolt of African Slaves in Iraq' (1999); Ghada Hashem Talhami on the term 'Zanj'.

nodes.label: Paper manufacture reaches Baghdad
nodes.full: The craft of making paper from pounded linen rag, learned from Central Asia, was set up in Baghdad in the 790s. Paper was far cheaper than parchment and harder to erase than papyrus, and within a generation the government had switched its records to it and the book trade had exploded. Few single technology transfers did more to shape a civilisation's intellectual life.
nodes.src: Jonathan Bloom, 'Paper Before Print' (2001); Ibn al-Nadim on the introduction of paper.

nodes.label: The canals that made Baghdad a river port
nodes.full: Baghdad sat where a set of transverse canals — the Nahr Isa chief among them — carried water and boats across from the Euphrates to the Tigris, giving the city access to both river systems, exactly the advantage Seleucia had held a thousand years before. The Nahrawan still watered the land to the east, and pontoon bridges of linked boats crossed the Tigris in the city.
nodes.src: Guy Le Strange, 'Baghdad During the Abbasid Caliphate' (1900); al-Ya'qubi, 'Kitāb al-Buldān'.

nodes.label: The instruments and the meridian measurement
nodes.full: Al-Ma'mun put astronomers to work with improved astrolabes, armillary spheres and large graduated arcs, checking the Greek parameters against fresh observation at Baghdad and Damascus. One team surveyed a stretch of the flat plain near Sinjar to measure the length of one degree of the meridian, and from it the size of the Earth — a field experiment, not an inherited number.
nodes.src: al-Biruni, 'Taḥdīd Nihāyāt al-Amākin'; the Ma'mūnic degree measurement in Ibn Yunus.

nodes.label: Building at the scale of an empire
nodes.full: The Round City was said to have taken a hundred thousand workers, and Samarra was a whole capital thrown up in a few years and half-abandoned within fifty. Both ran on the same kit: brickyards firing millions of units, a stucco industry turning out moulded panels by the thousand, and animal-driven wheels lifting water to the gardens. Speed and scale, at the cost of permanence.
nodes.src: Alastair Northedge, 'The Historical Topography of Samarra' (2005); K. A. C. Creswell, 'Early Muslim Architecture' vol. II (1940).

nodes.label: The centre of the world's routes
nodes.full: From Baghdad the roads ran everywhere that mattered: to China through Khurasan, to India through Basra, to the Volga and on to the Baltic — where hundreds of thousands of Abbasid silver coins have been dug up, paid out for northern furs and slaves — across the Sahara for West African gold, and west to Muslim Spain. The postmaster Ibn Khurradadhbih mapped the whole web in his road-book.
nodes.src: Ibn Khurradadhbih, 'Kitāb al-Masālik wa-l-Mamālik'; Thomas Noonan on the Islamic dirham in northern Europe.

nodes.label: The pilgrim road of Zubayda
nodes.full: The main hajj road ran fourteen hundred kilometres from Kufa across the desert to Mecca, and Harun al-Rashid's wife Zubayda endowed much of its infrastructure — paved approaches, milestones, walled cisterns, wells and rest-houses at a day's march apart. Iraq was the assembly point for the pilgrims of the entire eastern half of the Muslim world.
nodes.src: Saʿad al-Rashid, 'Darb Zubaydah: The Pilgrim Road from Kufa to Mecca' (1980).

nodes.label: Embassies and the prestige of the centre
nodes.full: Harun al-Rashid sent Charlemagne an Asian elephant, a brass water-clock and silks; envoys went to and came from Byzantium over ransoms and the buying of Greek manuscripts, and later from the Volga Bulgars and the Samanids of the east. When a Byzantine embassy was received in 917 the court laid on a display of a hundred lions and a silver tree with mechanical singing birds. Baghdad performed being the centre.
nodes.src: the reception of 917 in al-Khatib al-Baghdadi and Hilal al-Sabi, 'Rusūm Dār al-Khilāfa'; Einhard, 'Vita Karoli' 16.

nodes.label: The religious networks radiating out
nodes.full: Iraq was the switchboard of two faiths. The Jewish academies' written rulings went out to communities in Kairouan, Spain and the Rhineland, binding the diaspora to a Babylonian standard. The Church of the East ran its missions to Central Asia and India from the same city. And the Radhanite Jewish merchants, whose routes Ibn Khurradadhbih records, traded in a single circuit from Frankland to China.
nodes.src: Robert Brody, 'The Geonim of Babylonia' (1998); Ibn Khurradadhbih on the Rādhāniyya.

nodes.label: The fusion of the traditions
nodes.full: In Abbasid Iraq four inheritances were welded together: Persian statecraft and courtly manners, carried by the secretarial class and the Barmakids; Indian mathematics, astronomy and story; Greek philosophy, medicine and science; and the Arabic language and the religion of Islam. What came out was not any one of them but a new civilisation, and Baghdad was its crucible.
nodes.src: Dimitri Gutas, 'Greek Thought, Arabic Culture' (1998); Marshall Hodgson, 'The Venture of Islam' vol. I (1974).

nodes.label: The largest city outside China
nodes.full: In the ninth century Baghdad was, on any reckoning, one of the two or three largest cities on earth — perhaps half a million people, perhaps far more — and the richest, drawing grain, silver, silk, ideas and talent from three continents. Its people took it for granted that they lived at the centre of the inhabited world, and for a while they were close to right.
nodes.src: the size estimates in Jacob Lassner (1970) and Françoise Micheau; al-Ya'qubi's description of the city.

nodes.label: The making of an Arabic-speaking Iraq
nodes.full: Under the caliphs the population of Iraq slowly changed shape: a thin Arab settler class over a Persian and Aramaean peasantry, a vast servile population in the fields, the homes and the army, and a Jewish and Christian minority still perhaps a third of the whole. Through the ninth century conversion to Islam picked up speed and Arabic pushed Aramaic and Persian out of the towns.
nodes.src: Richard Bulliet, 'Conversion to Islam in the Medieval Period' (1979); Michael Morony, 'Iraq after the Muslim Conquest' (1984).

nodes.label: The rebellious granary
nodes.full: The province that fed the empire, housed its capital and generated its wealth was also the one it could never quite govern. Kharijites, the partisans of Ali, the Quran-reciters under Ibn al-Ash'ath, a string of Alid pretenders, the Zanj of the marshes, the Qaramita of the countryside — the risings never really stopped, and the canal economy that paid for everything was already slipping.
nodes.src: Hugh Kennedy, 'The Prophet and the Age of the Caliphates' (2004); Patricia Crone, 'The Nativist Prophets of Early Islamic Iran' (2012), on the rural movements.

nodes.label: The caliphate emptied out
nodes.full: By 945 the Abbasid caliph held the title and almost nothing else: the provinces were independent or lost, the treasury was empty, the army was a foreign guard, and the capital was contracting. When the Buyid Mu'izz al-Dawla marched in that December, the caliph became a stipendiary. Iraq was about to spend three centuries as the prize fought over by Buyids, Seljuks and, at the end, the Mongols.
nodes.src: Miskawayh, 'Tajārib al-Umam'; John Donohue, 'The Buwayhid Dynasty in Iraq' (2003).

nodes.label: al-Hasan al-Basri
nodes.full: A preacher and moralist in the Basra of the early Umayyad decades, he held the great crowd of the garrison city to account — for its luxury, its politics, its treatment of the poor — and taught a piety built on the fear of God and the shortness of life. Later Sunnis, Sufis and rationalist theologians all claimed him as a founder. He is the conscience of early Iraqi Islam.
nodes.src: the sermons preserved in Ibn Saʿd's 'Ṭabaqāt' and later collections; Suleiman Mourad, 'Early Islam between Myth and History: Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī' (2006).

nodes.label: The gaon of Sura
nodes.full: Head of one of the two academies, now in the capital, he ruled on questions of law and text sent by letter from Jewish communities as far off as Spain and India, drew the dues that funded the school, and presided at the assemblies where the tradition was taught. The greatest of the line, Saadia ben Joseph, translated the Bible into Arabic, wrote the first Jewish philosophy of religion, and broke the Karaite challenge.
nodes.src: Robert Brody, 'The Geonim of Babylonia and the Shaping of Medieval Jewish Culture' (1998).

nodes.label: Hunayn ibn Ishaq
nodes.full: A Nestorian Christian from al-Hira who mastered Greek, Syriac, Arabic and Persian, Hunayn ran the age's most exacting translation workshop, put the whole surviving body of Galen into usable Arabic, and served as physician to the caliphs. Al-Mutawakkil once jailed him for refusing to compound a poison. He fixed the technical vocabulary in which Arabic science would be written for centuries.
nodes.src: Hunayn's own 'Risāla' on his Galen translations; Ibn Abi Usaybia, 'ʿUyūn al-Anbāʾ'.

nodes.label: The qayna of Baghdad
nodes.full: A slave woman trained from girlhood in singing, the lute, poetry and quick talk, sold for the price of an estate, and hired out or kept to entertain the salons of the wealthy from behind a screen. She was expected to be brilliant company and to break hearts on the side. Al-Jahiz wrote a whole essay, half satire, on the economy of desire built around her.
nodes.src: al-Jahiz, 'Risālat al-Qiyān'; Kristina Richardson and others on enslaved musicians; Matthew Gordon & Kathryn Hain (eds.), 'Concubines and Courtesans' (2017).

nodes.label: The Zanj rebel
nodes.full: Brought in chains from the East African coast to strip the salt crust off the flats of lower Iraq for an absentee owner, he answered the call of the man the sources call the Master of the Zanj, took up arms, and for fourteen years lived as a soldier of a rebel state with its own coinage and its own capital. When al-Muwaffaq's army finally broke it in 883, the survivors were killed or re-enslaved.
nodes.src: al-Tabari III; Alexandre Popović, 'The Revolt of African Slaves in Iraq' (1999).
